Will auction-house deal structures (guarantees, irrevocable bids, third-party backing, financing, marketing) be sufficient to de-risk and complete a $100M+ public painting sale in the period?
A) Yes. The houses and their financial partners will be willing and able to assemble guarantees or equivalent support needed to get such a sale done publicly.
B) No. Risk appetite or financing support will be too limited to structure and execute a $100M+ public painting sale during the period.

Are the leading auction houses willing and able to structure guarantees or third-party backing that can bring a $100 million-level painting to public auction?
A) There is sufficient depth of bidding among global UHNW collectors/institutions to produce a competitive public sale at or above $100 million.
B) Bidder appetite is too thin or cautious for a painting to achieve a public $100 million result, even if a major work appears.

Is current buyer demand at the ultra-high end of the public painting auction market strong enough to support a publicly reported $100M+ result if an appropriate trophy work is offered before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Sufficient liquidity remains among top collectors, advisors, and institutions for the right work to attract bidding to or above $100M.
B) No. Demand at that level is too thin or cautious; even strong works would struggle to cross $100M in the current public auction environment.

Are there plausible near-term catalysts—estate dispersals, collection rebalancing, financial pressure, tax planning, or geopolitical relocation—that will release masterpiece paintings into public sale during the forecast window?
A) Yes. It is reasonable to expect at least one catalyst among deaths, divorces, debt needs, estate planning, or collection rotation to force or encourage a masterpiece to market soon.
B) No. Those catalysts may occur, but not often enough for this tiny set of ultra-trophy paintings; owners with such assets are usually not forced sellers and can wait for better conditions.

Will at least one owner of a painting plausibly capable of fetching about US$100 million or more choose public auction, rather than private sale or deferral, before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. At least one owner of a trophy-caliber painting will see public auction as attractive or necessary—because of estate dynamics, liquidity needs, competitive theater, price discovery, or confidence in the house’s marketing reach.
B) No. Owners of paintings in that value band will mostly prefer private transactions, museum arrangements, collateralized borrowing, or waiting for stronger conditions, so no qualifying work reaches public auction in time.
